titulo: The katakana that looks English — サービス, マンション, コンセント
subtitulo: Signs written in katakana read like borrowed English at a glance, which is exactly why a handful of them send you somewhere you did not mean to go
cena: You are in front of a sign with three lines of katakana on it, all of which look like English words you know, and the next hour depends on which one you actually believe.
frasePiso: Read the word, not the English word it sounds like. When you are not sure it exists here, open with 〜を探しています.

fatosDatados.afirmacao: Japan runs on convenience stores. The three big chains alone — Seven-Eleven, FamilyMart and Lawson — pass 55,000 branches nationwide, most of them open 24 hours, and they double as places to draw cash, pay bills, buy tickets and post parcels. For a traveller the useful corollary is that 'I cannot find one' is almost never the problem; the konbini is the default answer to a great many small searches.
fatosDatados.fonte: Japan Franchise Association (JFA), estatística de lojas de conveniência: as três maiores redes somam mais de 55 mil lojas no Japão, a maioria 24h, funcionando também como ponto de saque, pagamento de contas e retirada de encomendas.

fatosDatados.afirmacao: The cash machine you want is usually inside a convenience store. Seven Bank ATMs, in Seven-Eleven stores, and Japan Post Bank ATMs accept many foreign-issued cards around the clock, with on-screen English, while a bank's own branch ATM often will not take an overseas card at all. The practical rule: for cash, look for the konbini or the post office, not the bank.
fatosDatados.fonte: Seven Bank e Japan Post Bank: caixas eletrônicos que aceitam cartões estrangeiros 24h com menu em inglês; ATMs de agências bancárias comuns frequentemente recusam cartões emitidos fora do Japão.

steps.pt: Japan writes many signs in katakana, in words you think you know. Most are friendly. A few send you to the wrong place.
The frame: the thing, then wo sagashite imasu — I'm looking for. The trap: a マンション is no mansion, just an apartment block.
I'm looking for a pharmacy.

steps.promptPt: You need a proper pharmacy for a prescription, not just a shelf of drinks. Say what you are after. Speak now.
steps.pt: I'm looking for a pharmacy.

steps.es: 薬局ですか？ この先のドラッグストアにもありますよ。
steps.pt: A pharmacy? There's also a drugstore just up ahead.
steps.tts: 薬局ですか？ この先のドラッグストアにもありますよ。
steps.acao: Two different kinds of shop were just named. A 薬局 fills prescriptions; a ドラッグストア is the everyday one. Walk to the word that matches what you need.

steps.pt: Keep the frame, change the thing. And watch サービス: from a shopkeeper or receipt it means free, on the house — not a charge.

steps.promptPt: Your wallet is empty and the only machine you passed refused a foreign card. Open the search at the counter. Speak now.
steps.pt: I'm looking for a cash machine.
steps.tts: エーティーエムを探しています。

steps.es: コンビニのATMなら海外のカードも使えますよ。すぐそこです。
steps.pt: The konbini ATM takes foreign cards too. It's just over there.
steps.tts: コンビニのエーティーエムなら海外のカードも使えますよ。すぐそこです。
steps.acao: This is about the machine inside the convenience store, not the bank branch. Head for the konbini, not the bank door.

steps.promptPt: The card went through and you want to be sure there was no hidden fee. Say what you have, plainly. Speak now.
steps.es: すみません、現金しかないんです。
steps.pt: Sorry, I only have cash.
steps.tts: すみません、現金しかないんです。

steps.pt: コンセント is a power socket, not consent. Asking where the コンセント is means where can I plug in, nothing more.

steps.promptPt: Every door on this side of the building is marked 出口, exit. Ask for the other one. Speak now.
steps.pt: Where is the entrance?
The convenience store answers half these searches. Three big chains pass fifty-five thousand branches, most open all hours.

steps.promptPt: The small restaurant looks open but the lights are half down and it is three in the afternoon. Ask about the gap in the hours. Speak now.
steps.pt: Do you close in the afternoon?

steps.es: はい、二時から五時まで休憩です。夜は五時からです。
steps.pt: Yes, we break from two to five. We're open again from five in the evening.
steps.tts: はい、二時から五時まで休憩です。夜は五時からです。
steps.acao: Note the reopening time and come back then, or eat somewhere open now.

steps.pt: ビル is a building, not a bill. And バイキング on a restaurant sign is an all-you-can-eat buffet, nothing to do with Vikings.

steps.promptPt: At the drugstore counter, you have a dry cough and no idea what the box is called. Speak now.
steps.es: 咳の薬を探しています。
steps.pinyin: se-ki no ku-SU-ri o sa-ga-shi-te i-MAS
steps.pt: I'm looking for something for a cough.
steps.tts: 咳の薬を探しています。

steps.pt: クレーム is a complaint, not a cream. If a sign points to the クレーム counter, that is where problems go, not desserts.

steps.promptPt: There is a socket on the wall by your table and your phone is at four percent. Ask whether you may use it. Speak now.
steps.es: ここで充電してもいいですか？
steps.pinyin: ko-ko de joo-DEN shi-te mo II des ka
steps.pt: Can I charge my phone here?
steps.tts: ここで充電してもいいですか？

steps.pt: For cash, use the konbini or post office, not the bank. Their machines take foreign cards in English, all hours; banks often won't.

steps.promptPt: Someone is inside with the lights on and the shutter still down. Open politely and ask about opening time. Speak now.
steps.es: すみません、何時に開きますか？
steps.pt: Excuse me, what time do you open?
steps.tts: すみません、何時に開きますか？

steps.promptPt: You are holding what you chose and there are three counters, none obviously the paying one. Speak now.
steps.pt: Where is the till?

steps.promptPt: Someone steps towards you the moment you walk in and you have not decided anything. Speak now.
steps.es: ちょっと見てもいいですか？
steps.pinyin: chot-to MI-te mo II des ka
steps.pt: Can I just have a look?
steps.tts: ちょっと見てもいいですか？

steps.es: 薬局を探しています。入口はどこですか？ お昼は休憩ですか？
steps.pinyin: yak-KYO-ku o sa-ga-shi-te i-MAS. i-ri-GU-chi wa DO-ko des ka. o-HI-ru wa kyoo-KEI des ka
steps.pt: Shadow the three sentences that get you through a written sign.
steps.tts: 薬局を探しています。入口はどこですか？ お昼は休憩ですか？

steps.pt: B10 done. マンション, サービス, コンセント, ビル, バイキング — five katakana words that now say what they actually say.

aprofundar.titulo: Five katakana words that are not what they look like

secoes.titulo: The five that cost you an afternoon
secoes.corpo: マンション is an ordinary apartment building, not a mansion. サービス means free, on the house, when a shopkeeper says it. コンセント is a power socket. ビル is a building. バイキング is an all-you-can-eat buffet. When you are not sure the thing exists nearby, open with 〜を探しています rather than asking straight for a place.

exemplos.pt: I'm looking for a cash machine.

secoes.titulo: 探しています opens a search, どこですか asks for a place
secoes.corpo: 〜はどこですか asks for somewhere you already believe is there — 出口, トイレ, 駅. 〜を探しています opens a search that might come back empty, which is the honest shape when you do not yet know whether this street has a pharmacy at all. The particle を and the ending 探しています stay put; only the thing before them moves.

secoes.titulo: 薬局, ドラッグストア and the cough
secoes.corpo: A 薬局 has a pharmacist and fills prescriptions; a ドラッグストア is the big everyday shop with cosmetics, snacks and over-the-counter medicine. For a cough or a cold, either works and the counter will choose the box — you name the symptom, 咳の薬 or 風邪薬, not the drug.

secoes.titulo: For cash, the konbini and the post office
secoes.corpo: Japan still runs heavily on cash, and the machine that will take your foreign card is usually inside a convenience store or a post office, not a bank branch. Seven Bank and Japan Post Bank ATMs work around the clock with an English menu. A bank's own branch ATM often refuses an overseas card outright, which is a quirk of the machine, not of your card.

permissao: You are allowed to misread a sign. Everyone who reads a second language reads it through the first one, and the fix is not vocabulary lists — it is knowing the handful of katakana words that lie, and asking out loud about the next one with 〜を探しています.
espelho: Anyone who has stood in front of a closed shutter in the afternoon in their own country, phone in hand, trying to work out whether a place is shut for a break or shut for good, already knows this feeling. The only new part is that here the sign tells you, in words that look borrowed from English.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You ask for a 薬局 and are pointed to a big bright shop full of cosmetics and snacks with a medicine shelf at the back.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: My accent got in the way and they misunderstood me.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: The word landed. A 薬局 has a pharmacist and a prescription counter; a ドラッグストア is the everyday shop that also sells over-the-counter medicine. Nothing went wrong except which word you reached for, and for a cough the drugstore is often the right place anyway.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Pick the word for what you need: 薬局 if you are filling a prescription, ドラッグストア or just 咳の薬を探しています for something over the counter. If you are not sure it is nearby, open with 探しています.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You stop treating a clean answer as a failed one, and you arrive at the right counter the first time.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not a hard line — many drugstores have a 薬局 counter inside them, and plenty of small pharmacies stock everyday items too. The word tells you whether a pharmacist is on duty, not whether they sell plasters.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You go to draw cash and the bank's machine on the corner rejects your card, but the one inside the convenience store works fine.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: Something is wrong with my card, or with me as a foreigner.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: Japan still leans on cash, and the machines set up for foreign cards are the konbini ones — Seven Bank inside Seven-Eleven, and Japan Post Bank — which run around the clock with an English menu. A bank branch's own ATM frequently does not accept overseas cards at all. It is a difference between machines, not a judgement about you.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: For cash, look for the convenience store or the post office, not the bank. Draw a little extra while you are there, because small places may be cash only.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You keep a small cash cushion for exactly these moments and stop reading a machine's refusal as a personal one.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not every bank ATM refuses foreign cards, and in the big cities cashless payment is spreading fast. This is a reason to know where the konbini machine is, not to assume banks never work.

clique.desconto: Nobody gave you a word for each thing you went looking for. You kept one opening and changed only what came after it — and the opening also survived the katakana words that lied to you.
clique.piso: Next time a sign looks like English, you will not trust the resemblance. You will say what you are looking for and let them correct the word.
